                    ### Question
                    A 50-year-old man comes to the emergency department for evaluation of right-sided facial weakness that he noticed after waking up. One month ago, he also experienced right-sided neck pain and headache that began after returning from a hunting trip to New Hampshire the week before. He took ibuprofen to relieve symptoms, which subsided a week later. He has a 5-year history of hypertension controlled with drug therapy. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 35 years and he drinks two beers daily. His vital signs are within the normal range. Physical examination shows right-sided drooping of the upper and lower half of the face. The patient has difficulties smiling and he is unable to close his right eye. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Western blot
opb. Polymerase chain reaction of the facial skin
opc. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis
opd. Enzyme‑linked immunosorbent assay
ope. Noncontrast CT

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with right-sided facial weakness, which suggests peripheral facial nerve involvement, commonly seen in Bell's palsy. Given the recent travel to New Hampshire and symptoms of neck pain and headache, Lyme disease is a strong consideration. The standard diagnostic approach for suspected Lyme disease with neurological involvement, such as facial palsy, begins with an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for Lyme disease screening. If ELISA is positive or equivocal, it is followed by a Western blot for confirmation. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis is typically reserved for cases with more severe neurological symptoms or when central nervous system involvement is suspected. Noncontrast CT is not routinely used for diagnosing Lyme disease but may be considered to rule out other causes of facial paralysis if clinical suspicion is low. Therefore, the most appropriate next step in diagnosis is an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for Lyme disease screening.
